flashcards.q: Define VaR precisely and give the parametric formula with z-values.
flashcards.a: Loss threshold exceeded with probability 1-alpha. Parametric (normal): VaR = -(mu - z*sigma)*V ~ z*sigma*V for short horizons. One-sided z: 95%=1.645, 97.5%=1.96, 99%=2.326.

flashcards.q: What does VaR NOT tell you?
flashcards.a: Anything about losses beyond the quantile - magnitude of the worst 1% is invisible, and it can be far worse than VaR itself. ES answers that: E[loss | loss >= VaR].

flashcards.q: State the four coherence axioms and which one VaR violates.
flashcards.a: Monotonicity, translation invariance, positive homogeneity, subadditivity (Artzner et al 1999). VaR violates subadditivity: two digitals each losing $100M w.p. 0.7% have individual 99%-VaR = 0 but joint 99%-VaR ~ $100M > 0+0.

flashcards.q: Compare ES 97.5% to VaR 99% under normality and under fat tails.
flashcards.a: Normal: ES97.5 = 2.338 sigma ~ VaR99 = 2.326 sigma - nearly identical capital. Fat tails (t-dist): ES grows faster than VaR because it averages the whole tail region, so it properly penalizes heavy-tailed books. This asymmetry is the FRTB rationale.

flashcards.q: What did FRTB change vs the 1996 market risk framework?
flashcards.a: 99%/10-day VaR -> Expected Shortfall at 97.5% on liquidity horizons 10-120 days by factor class; added sensitivities-based Standardized Approach as floor, P&L attribution test (unresolved trades < 10%), NMRF add-ons for unmodellable factors. Finalized Jan 2019; EU live from 2024, US phasing 2025-26.

flashcards.q: Kupiec POF test: formula shape, distribution, critical value.
flashcards.a: LR = -2 ln[(1-p)^(T-x) p^x] + 2 ln[(1-x/T)^(T-x)(x/T)^x] comparing observed exception frequency to hypothesized p; chi-square(1); reject at 5% if LR > 3.841.

flashcards.q: Expected exceptions per year at 99% and 97.5% over 250 days, and why power still fails.
flashcards.a: 99%: 2.5/yr; 97.5%: 6.25/yr. Distinguishing p=1% from p=3% reliably needs thousands of observations, so Type II errors dominate at high confidence exactly where models are thinnest.

flashcards.q: Why do exceptions cluster and which test detects it?
flashcards.a: Volatility clustering (GARCH): breaches arrive in runs after regime shifts (Oct 2008). Breaks iid Bernoulli assumption behind Kupiec. Christoffersen independence LR compares P(exc|no exc yesterday) vs P(exc|exc yesterday). Fix structurally: GARCH/EWMA-filtered conditional VaR.

flashcards.q: Basel traffic-light backtesting zones and consequences.
flashcards.a: Green 0-4 exceptions/year at 99%, yellow 5-9, red >=10. Yellow raises capital via plus-factor (multiplier k rises from 3 toward 4); red presumes model inadequacy -> k=4 mandatory plus revalidation/remediation.

flashcards.q: Historical simulation pros/cons vs filtered historical simulation.
flashcards.a: HS: no distributional assumption, captures realized fat tails, full revaluation handles nonlinearity - but tail estimated from only 2-5 observations in a 250-day window, stale data lingers, reacts late (echo effects). FHS: GARCH-filter residuals then bootstrap - responsive vol + historical tail shapes; desk standard.

flashcards.q: Four stress-test families and what reverse stress testing adds.
flashcards.a: Historical replay (2008 week, Mar-2020), hypothetical macro (CCAR severe adverse: unemployment +5-6pp, equities -50%), sensitivity shocks (+300bp rates, +500bp spreads), reverse stress (solve for the breach combination). Reverse reveals vulnerability magnitudes instead of confirming chosen fears; expected under ICAAP/Pillar 2.

flashcards.q: What is the FRTB P&L attribution test comparing, and what's the failure consequence?
flashcards.a: Risk-theoretical (hypothetical) P&L from the risk model's factor set vs front-office actual P&L, via Spearman/KS tests plus unresolved-trades ratio < 10%. Failure makes the desk ineligible for internal models - falls back to standardized capital.
